summary: This is a mechanistic evidence review (dated 4 November 2026) evaluating the proposed cascade from extracranial venous obstruction (specifically left brachiocephalic/aortosternal compression) through lymphovenous pressure loading to impaired neuro-lymphatic/glymphatic brain clearance, with potential fluid egress via palatal and mastoid pathways. The review synthesizes human case reports, animal experiments, and anatomical studies across 30 references, concluding that individual mechanistic links have experimental support but the complete end-to-end sequence has not been demonstrated in a single human study. It is a secondary evidence synthesis relevant to TRL 1–2 for the overall proposed cascade, with some component links at TRL 2–3.

content_blocks.title: Cover Page & Central Finding
content_blocks.content: Title: 'Extracranial Venous Obstruction and Neuro-Lymphatic Clearance — Mechanistic evidence review | 4 November 2026.' Central finding: Substantial evidence exists for several individual links between venous outflow impairment, abnormal CSF handling, and lymphatic dysfunction. However, the complete sequence from aortosternal compression to persistent cerebral clearance deficit and visible oral or postauricular fluid discharge has NOT been demonstrated in a single human study. This leaves an investigable hypothesis, not biological impossibility.

content_blocks.title: Evidence Assessment Summary Table (Page 1)
content_blocks.content:
Five proposed mechanistic links with evidence assessments:
1. Left brachiocephalic obstruction → cranial venous reflux: Demonstrated in human cases. High-flow dialysis cases establish causality in that setting; isolated external compression requires separate assessment. [refs 1-4]
2. High venous outlet pressure → lymphatic congestion: Direct pressure/flow experiments and human central-vein obstruction cases support this mechanism. Pump adaptation and collateral flow can compensate. [refs 5-9]
3. Venous impairment → meningeal lymphatic/brain clearance impairment: Experimental causal evidence, with supportive human imaging associations. [refs 10,11]
4. CSF-associated transport through palatal pathways: Anatomically traced in mice; supportive tracer observations in two macaques. Human pathological oral leakage remains unproven. [ref 18]
5. Mastoid emissary route → external lymph/CSF pooling: Venous connections well established. Proposed nonvascular leak pathway remains unresolved. [refs 22-25]

content_blocks.title: Search Scope and Limits
content_blocks.content: Targeted web-assisted searches covered PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central full text, and OpenAlex bibliographic records, with journal-page verification and reference tracing. Queries combined brachiocephalic/aortosternal obstruction, jugular reflux, lymphovenous pressure, glymphatic clearance, compartment syndrome, palatine/incisive pathways, and mastoid/emissary anatomy. Europe PMC was unavailable; Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were not directly searched. No PRISMA process claimed. Priority given to original human studies, animal experiments, and anatomical work. Case reports establish possibility but not prevalence. Review evaluates mechanisms only; does not diagnose individual patients.

content_blocks.title: Section 01: The Venous Bottleneck — Anatomy and Hemodynamics
content_blocks.content: The left brachiocephalic vein carries left jugular and subclavian venous return across the superior mediastinum. Compression between sternum and adjacent great arteries can raise resistance downstream of the left venous angle. Respiratory change in caliber is documented in aortosternal compression. Hemodynamic model: P_upstream − P_downstream = Q × R_effective. A narrowed segment raises resistance, but parallel collaterals can lower total resistance. Sustained cranial hypertension depends on resulting pressures and flow distribution (contralateral jugular drainage, vertebral pathways, venous dominance, valve function). Retrograde pressure transmission does not require continuous retrograde blood flow. Key caveat: a normal right-atrial or general central venous pressure cannot exclude elevated pressure upstream of a left brachiocephalic stenosis.

content_blocks.title: Human Evidence Table: Venous Bottleneck Studies
content_blocks.content:
Four human studies reviewed:
1. Giglio et al., 2022 [1]: Two cases with breathing-dependent aortosternal venous compression documented by CT and venography. Establishes lesion and dynamic nature; did not measure brain solute clearance.
2. Arcot & DeOrchis, 2024 [2]: 'Syndrome Sinistre' — hypothesis-generating clinical/anatomical report proposing neurological consequences of left brachiocephalic compression when collaterals are inadequate. Shows cranial reflux and improved venous flow after stenting. No controlled efficacy study.
3. Herzig et al., 2013 [3]: Two dialysis patients with neurological complications from brachiocephalic obstruction and jugular reflux. One had recurrent myoclonic seizures with stent occlusion, improved after reopening — informative within-patient recurrence/reversal observation.
4. Kim et al., 2018 [4]: Two dialysis-access cases with intracranial reflux mimicking dural arteriovenous fistula. One improved after angioplasty/stenting; other developed fatal intracranial bleeding. Neither measured lymphatic drainage.
Transferability note: Dialysis access adds substantial inflow to an obstructed venous circuit; these cases do not establish how often isolated aortosternal compression produces the same pressure burden.

content_blocks.title: Section 02: Lymphovenous Afterload and the 'Pressure Lock'
content_blocks.content:
The venous angle is a lymphatic outlet into blood. If the receiving vein is pressurized, the terminal lymphatic system must work against greater afterload. Competent valves resist blood reflux but cannot guarantee lymph emptying against any downstream pressure. Head drainage is bilateral and does not all traverse one left-sided outlet.

Illustrative one-way outlet model (not validated patient-specific): Q_LV(t) ≈ max{0, [P_L(t) − P_V(t) − P_open] / R_LV(t)}

Key experimental evidence:
1. Brace & Valenzuela (sheep, n=6): Thoracic duct flow preserved over initial pressure range, then fell and stopped at 25.6 ± 4.2 mmHg. Model-specific result, not a human diagnostic threshold. [ref 6]
2. Gabel & Drake (sheep, n=4): Increased neck venous pressure produced matching changes in pressure at lung lymphatic-thoracic duct junction. Demonstrates upstream lymphatic loading from venous hypertension. [ref 7]
3. Lu et al. (animal model, tricuspid regurgitation): Central venous pressure rose from ~4.2 to 10.1 mmHg; thoracic duct flow increased ~8-11-fold. Pressure, caliber, and wall thickness also increased. Elevated venous pressure does not inevitably produce immediate zero-flow lymphatic stasis. [ref 8]
4. Davis et al.: Isolated lymphangions demonstrate increased contractility in response to afterload. [ref 28]

Human example: Chick et al. — brachiocephalic and axillary venous occlusion with engorged, disrupted thoracic duct and chylothorax. Venous reconstruction plus duct embolization resolved the leak. Supports venous-lymphatic coupling; combined intervention cannot isolate which component produced benefit. Thoracic leakage is not direct evidence of cerebral or palatal leak. [ref 5]

content_blocks.title: Section 03: Brain Clearance and Intracranial Compliance
content_blocks.content:
Compartment distinction: Glymphatic transport involves CSF, brain interstitial fluid, and perivascular spaces. Meningeal and extracranial lymphatics are endothelial-lined vessels carrying fluid/solutes toward lymph nodes and venous outlets. They interact but do not form one uninterrupted pipe.

Key studies:
1. El Kamouh et al. (2026, Nature Neuroscience): Combined human IIH imaging with bilateral jugular ligation in mice. Venous obstruction produced transient pressure elevation, edema, altered clearance, and meningeal lymphatic regression; recovery involved remodeling; lymphatic depletion impaired recovery. Human contrast analyses: 16 IIH patients vs. 19 controls; perisinusal enhancement was a surrogate, not direct lymph-flow measurement. BMI and treatment differences limit causal interpretation. [ref 10]
2. Eide et al. (2021, Brain Communications): Intrathecal gadobutrol followed in 15 IIH patients and 15 reference individuals for 48 hours. Brain tracer clearance was delayed in IIH. Human kinetic evidence of impaired clearance without identifying extracranial cause. [ref 11]

Monro-Kellie update: V_skull ≈ V_cells/solids + V_ISF + V_blood + V_free CSF + V_meningeal structures/fluid; C_intracranial = dV/dP. Interstitial water already included in 'brain volume' must not be double-counted as extra lymph compartment.

CSF absorption model: Q_CSF→venous = max{0, (P_CSF − P_sinus − P_threshold)/R}. Raising sinus pressure reduces driving gradient unless CSF pressure rises too. Jugular-ligation experiments demonstrate reduced CSF absorption. [ref 30]

Aspelund et al.: Impaired macromolecule clearance in lymphatic-deficient mice without increased interstitial pressure or water content — protein clearance and pressure can dissociate. [ref 14]

'Pressure lock' is best treated as an operational hypothesis of insufficient throughput under adverse downstream conditions, not an all-or-none universal state.

content_blocks.title: Section 04: Palatal and Nasopharyngeal Egress
content_blocks.content:
Palatal route experimental support:
1. Jin et al. (2025, Nature): CSF-associated transport traced through lymphatics accompanying the greater palatine pathway and through nasal lymphatics crossing the incisive foramen to the hard-palate plexus in mice. Downstream transport reached superficial cervical/submandibular nodes. Tracer near incisive and greater palatine foramina also observed in two macaques. These were contained drainage pathways, NOT demonstrations of free discharge into the mouth. [ref 18]
2. Yoon et al. (2024, Nature): Nasopharyngeal lymphatic plexus connecting intracranial/perineural routes to deep cervical nodes in mice. Downstream collecting-vessel smooth muscle influenced transport. Supports regional extracranial control of CSF drainage and multiple parallel outflow routes. [ref 17]

Human evidence:
- Eide et al. (2018): Cervical-node enhancement after intrathecal tracer administration — supports human CNS-to-cervical clearance connection. [ref 19]
- Yagmurlu et al.: Lymphatic structures in dura around jugular foramen and connections toward cervical lymphatics in human anatomical specimens. Anatomical continuity does not measure flow. [ref 21]
- Rasmussen et al.: Palatine-tonsil tracer injection in human pilot study visualized cervical lymphatic drainage, changed with head-down tilt. CSF-to-node tracing separately demonstrated in swine. Human tonsillar experiment did NOT trace CSF from brain to mouth. [ref 20]

Key mechanistic inference: If one outlet becomes high resistance, flow may redistribute to lower-resistance channels. An oral leak would require additional evidence of a communication or barrier defect, source-specific transport, or sufficient local filtration with impaired removal.

Protein/ectopic filtrate caution: 'Denatured,' 'misfolded,' and 'aggregated' describe different molecular properties requiring appropriate assays. A visible deposit or nonspecific protein concentration cannot establish CNS origin.

content_blocks.title: Section 05: Mastoid Pathways — Observations vs. Unresolved Questions
content_blocks.content:
Human dissection and MRI establish mastoid emissary vein connects sigmoid-sinus region with posterior auricular/occipital and suboccipital venous networks. Reis et al. dissected 15 injected cadaveric specimens; Tsutsumi et al. evaluated 96 patients by MRI. Channel sizes vary substantially. [refs 22,23]

Observation | What it establishes | What remains unresolved
--- | --- | ---
Contrast in mastoid emissary channel | Patency/opacification of venous connection; direction requires temporal/flow information | Whether fluid has left the vessel; whether extravascular component is CSF, lymph, or local edema
Enlarged emissary veins | Possible collateral pathway; may reflect normal variation | Driving pressure, adequacy of decompression, causal relationship to symptoms
Mastoid air-cell fluid | Fluid in normally aerated middle-ear/mastoid compartment | Its origin and any communication with CSF or lymphatic structures
Postauricular or scalp swelling | Regional excess fluid or soft-tissue abnormality | Whether cause is local filtration, venous congestion, lymphatic obstruction, or separate leak

Key finding: No direct human tracer evidence of proposed brain-to-scalp lymphatic leakage through mastoid emissary foramen was identified in this search.

Adjacent evidence:
- Jung et al. (2020): 115 postoperative neurocritical-care patients; 61 developed mastoid effusion. Measured ICP improved prediction of effusion, but multiple confounders. Supports association, not identified emissary leak. [ref 24]
- Jianan Lu et al. (2026): Impaired glymphatic/lymphatic MRI markers after subarachnoid hemorrhage. Mastoid air-cell fluid in 53.8% of chronic-hydrocephalus subgroup, correlated inversely with lymphatic signal. Abstract only; does not establish fluid origin or emissary route. [ref 25]

content_blocks.title: Section 06: Blind Spots in Neurological and Radiological Assessment
content_blocks.content:
Seven identified blind spots with research responses:
1. Brain-only field of view: Causative outlet lesion may lie at lower neck or mediastinum. Response: Link head, neck, and thoracic venous anatomy.
2. Static caliber as surrogate for flow: Breathing, position, collateral recruitment, and injection conditions can alter appearances. Response: Measure direction, transit, respiratory dependence, and pressure.
3. Single central venous pressure: Right-atrial pressure need not equal local pressure upstream of a stenosis. Response: Compare local upstream/downstream measurements.
4. Global ICP as only endpoint: Solute clearance may change without proportional change in mean pressure. Response: Assess clearance kinetics, compliance, and regional tissue fluid.
5. MRI surrogate specificity: ALPS indices and meningeal enhancement do not directly measure sealed lymphatic lumen or total clearance. Response: Use complementary methods.
6. Species and drainage territory: Palatal routes best mapped in animals; human outlet anatomy and relative flow fractions incompletely defined. Response: Map bilateral cervical pathways.
7. Pooling versus fluid provenance: Edema, lymphatic transport, venous blood, and CSF fistula can be adjacent. Response: Require anatomical continuity and source identification.

Measurement cautions:
- Schilling et al. (2025): White-matter geometry and crossing/undulating fibers can substantially confound DTI-ALPS measurements. A low index cannot independently diagnose 'glymphatic failure.' [ref 27]
- El Kamouh et al. (2026): Human perisinusal enhancement treated as indirect marker only. [ref 10]
- Iliff et al. vs. Smith et al.: Contested physical basis of intraparenchymal transport — paravascular clearance pathway (Iliff) vs. diffusion-dominated, aquaporin-4-independent solute transport (Smith). [refs 12, 29]

content_blocks.title: Section 07: Testable Integrated Model — Link-by-Link Testing Framework
content_blocks.content:
Regional mass balance: dV_interstitial/dt = J_filtration − Q_lymphatic removal

Five links to test with strengthening evidence and limiting results:
1. Hemodynamically significant obstruction | Reproducible upstream pressure elevation, altered transit/reflux, dynamic compression at same lesion | Caliber narrowing with preserved drainage and no relevant gradient under symptom-associated conditions
2. Lymphatic outlet loading | Mapped cervical outlet plus delayed lymph transit, upstream distension, or adverse lymph-to-vein pressure relation | Preserved lymph transport despite venous abnormality
3. Effect on CNS clearance | Abnormal tracer washout or validated kinetic endpoint temporally related to outlet problem | Normal clearance across sufficiently sensitive, appropriately timed measurements
4. Specific palatal or mastoid pooling route | Documented pathway continuity and source-specific fluid movement into affected tissue/space | Local source explaining collection, or absent continuity on adequately targeted assessment
5. Reversibility and causation | After clinically justified treatment: improvement in pressures, clearance kinetics, and pooling in predicted order | Symptom change without predicted physiological changes; persistence of clearance defect after verified decompression

Proposed study design requirements: Distinguish isolated aortosternal compression from dialysis-associated high-flow disease; enroll appropriate comparison group; record position, respiration, hydration, medications; map both cervical drainage territories; prespecify physiological and clinical endpoints; serial measures to distinguish immediate pressure relief from slower lymphatic remodeling.

Clinical translation caveat: Evidence for mechanism supports careful assessment of suspected obstruction. It does not establish that venous stenting, lymphatic bypass, massage, or suction will correct an individual's problem.

key_findings: The complete sequence from aortosternal compression to persistent cerebral clearance deficit and visible oral or postauricular fluid discharge has NOT been demonstrated in a single human study — it remains an investigable hypothesis.
Left brachiocephalic obstruction → cranial venous reflux is demonstrated in human cases (dialysis setting); isolated external compression requires separate assessment (refs 1-4).

High venous outlet pressure → lymphatic congestion is supported by direct pressure/flow animal experiments: thoracic duct flow stopped at 25.6 ± 4.2 mmHg in sheep (Brace & Valenzuela, n=6); compensatory 8-11-fold flow increase also documented (Lu et al.).

Venous impairment → meningeal lymphatic/brain clearance impairment has experimental causal evidence (bilateral jugular ligation in mice, El Kamouh et al. 2026, Nature Neuroscience) and supportive human imaging associations (16 IIH patients vs. 19 controls).
Impaired glymphatic clearance in IIH demonstrated by intrathecal gadobutrol kinetics in 15 IIH patients vs. 15 references over 48 hours (Eide et al. 2021).

CSF-associated transport through palatal pathways anatomically traced in mice (Jin et al. 2025, Nature); supportive tracer observations in only two macaques; human pathological oral leakage remains unproven.

Mastoid emissary venous connections are well established (15 cadaveric specimens, 96-patient MRI study), but proposed nonvascular brain-to-scalp lymphatic leak pathway through mastoid emissary foramen has no direct human tracer evidence.

Mastoid air-cell fluid occurred in 53.8% of chronic-hydrocephalus subgroup after subarachnoid hemorrhage and correlated inversely with lymphatic signal (Lu et al. 2026), but fluid origin and emissary route not established.
DTI-ALPS measurements are substantially confounded by white-matter geometry (Schilling et al. 2025) — a low index cannot independently diagnose glymphatic failure.
Protein clearance and pressure can dissociate: lymphatic-deficient mice showed impaired macromolecule clearance without increased interstitial pressure or water content (Aspelund et al.).
The physical basis of intraparenchymal transport remains contested: paravascular bulk flow (Iliff et al.) vs. diffusion-dominated, aquaporin-4-independent transport (Smith et al.).

A prospective study to test the full cascade should distinguish isolated aortosternal compression from dialysis-associated high-flow disease, enroll comparison groups, and prespecify physiological and clinical endpoints including clearance kinetics.
